payload.markdown:
Malay uses the same 26 letters you already read. The trap is that it uses them differently. English **e** has several sounds; Malay **e** has two. English **c** is sometimes *k*, sometimes *s*; Malay **c** is always the *ch* in *church*. Read *terima kasih* with English vowel rules and you get "teh-RYE-mah KAY-see" — nobody in a mamak will turn around. Read it with the table below and you get "tuh-ree-mah kah-seeh", which works.

Two rules carry most of the load.

**Vowels are short and pure.** *a* is the *a* in *father*, *i* is *ee* in *see*, *u* is *oo* in *food*, *o* is *o* in *low* with no *w* sliding off the end. No diphthongs — do not glide.

**Consonants are single-valued.** *c* is always *ch*. *g* is always hard, as in *go* — never the soft *g* of *giant*. *j* is the *j* in *jug*. *ng* is the *ng* in *singer*, with no hard *g* after it; *ngg* is the *ng* in *finger*, with one. *ny* is the *ny* in *canyon*. *sy* is *sh*. *kh* is the Scottish *ch* in *loch*.

Two endings need practice. A word-final **-a** softens to a short *uh* in everyday Peninsular speech: *saya* is "sa-yuh", not "sa-yah". And a word-final **-k** is not a *k* at all — it is a stop in the throat, the sound you make in the middle of "uh-oh". *tidak* comes out "tida'" with the mouth closing and nothing released.

Stress is light and even. Most speakers lean slightly on the second-last syllable, but leaning wrong costs you far less than mispronouncing a *c* or a final *a*.

cards.back: Always hard, as in *go*: goo-lah. Never the soft *g* of *giant*.
*ng* = *singer*, no hard g (*dengan*). *ngg* = *finger*, one hard g (*tangga*).
Softens to a short *uh* in everyday Peninsular speech: *saya* = sa-yuh.
A stop in the throat, nothing released: *tidak* = tee-dah'.
Usually short *uh* as in *about* (*besar* = buh-sar); sometimes *e* in *bed* (*meja* = meh-ja).
*sy* = *sh* in *shop* (*syarikat*). *kh* = Scottish *ch* in *loch* (*khabar*), often softened to *k*.
*o* in *low*, with no *w* gliding off the end: *kopi* = ko-pee.
A tapped r, as in Spanish. Word-finally it is often dropped: *besar* can sound like buh-sa.
Light and fairly even; many speakers lean slightly on the second-last syllable.
*i* = *ee* in *see* (*ikan*). *u* = *oo* in *food* (*susu*). Short and pure, no glide.

payload.title: Reading terima kasih off the table
payload.markdown:
Your phrasebook lists *terima kasih* (thank you). Here is the whole word taken apart with the table, letter group by letter group.

| Chunk | Letters | Rule | Sound |
|---|---|---|---|
| te- | t, e | **e** is the short *uh* of *about* | tuh |
| -ri- | r, i | **r** tapped; **i** is *ee* in *see* | ree |
| -ma | m, a | **a** is *a* in *father*; it ends the word *terima*, so in relaxed speech it may soften to *uh* | mah |
| ka- | k, a | same **a** | kah |
| -sih | s, i, h | **i** is *ee*; final **h** is breathed | seeh |

Put together: **tuh-ree-mah kah-seeh**. Stress sits lightly on the second-last syllable of each word — *tuh-REE-mah*, *KAH-seeh*.

Now the same method on a word you will meet at the counter. *ais* (iced) is not English "ace": **a** is *a* in *father*, **i** is *ee*, so it is "ah-ees", two syllables, not one. And *kopi* is "ko-pee", not "KOH-pye".

Run the method on any new word: split it, apply the table to each chunk, then check the two endings — a final **-a** softens, a final **-k** stops.

assessments.explanation: Malay **c** is always the *ch* in *China*, and **a** is the *a* in *father* in both syllables. *cakap* is chah-kahp. Option a applies the English habit of reading *c* as *k*; option c reads it as *s*, the other English value; option d invents a second vowel value the word does not have.

options.text: The letter g is always hard, as in go.
The letters ng are pronounced with a hard g after them, as in finger.
A word-final a often softens to a short uh in everyday Peninsular speech.
The letter e has only one pronunciation in Malay.

assessments.explanation: The table gives g one value only (hard, as in *go*), softens word-final *a* to *uh* (*saya* = sa-yuh), and makes word-final *k* a throat stop (*tidak* = tida'). Option b confuses *ng* with *ngg* — *finger* is the *ngg* row. Option d is wrong because *e* has two values: short *uh* in *besar*, *e* in *bed* in *meja*.

assessments.prompt: A friend reads *tangga* (stairs) aloud as "tan-gah" and *dengan* (with) as "deng-gahn". Using section 1 of your phrasebook, explain what they got wrong in each word and give the correct reading of both.

answer_key.reference_answer: *tangga* is spelled ngg, which is the *ng* of *finger* — one hard g after the ng — so it is "tahng-gah", not "tan-gah". *dengan* is spelled ng, which is the *ng* of *singer* with no hard g, so it is "duh-ngahn", not "deng-gahn". The friend has swapped the two rows of the table.

rubric.criterion: Correctly distinguishes ng from ngg using the phrasebook's two rows
rubric.excellent: States that ng is the *ng* in *singer* with no hard g and ngg is the *ng* in *finger* with one hard g, and applies each to the right word.
rubric.acceptable: States that the two spellings sound different and names *singer* and *finger*, but mixes up which word gets which.
rubric.poor: Treats ng and ngg as the same sound, or says nothing about the hard g.

rubric.criterion: Gives a correct reading for both words
rubric.excellent: Gives "tahng-gah" for *tangga* and "duh-ngahn" for *dengan*, with the vowels right as well as the ng.
rubric.acceptable: Gets the ng/ngg distinction right in both but slips on one vowel, such as writing "deng-ngahn".
rubric.poor: Gives readings that keep the friend's original error in one or both words.

rubric.criterion: Names the specific rule being broken rather than saying 'it sounds wrong'
rubric.excellent: Points at the two table rows by name and says the friend has applied the ngg rule to an ng word and the reverse.
rubric.acceptable: Says the friend used the wrong row of the table without identifying which row applies to which word.
rubric.poor: Offers no rule, only a corrected pronunciation.

assessments.reason: Section 1 gives ng as in singer (dengan) and ngg as in finger (tangga), so the friend swapped the rows.

payload.belief: Malay is written in the Latin alphabet, so I can just read it the way I read English.
payload.why_it_seems_right: The letters are identical and most of the words look familiar on the page. *Meja*, *kopi*, *susu* — nothing in the spelling warns you that a rule is about to change under you.
payload.what_is_true: Malay shares the alphabet but not the letter values. *c* is always *ch*, never *k* or *s*. *g* is always hard. Word-final *a* softens to *uh* and word-final *k* becomes a throat stop. Read *terima kasih* with English rules and you produce "teh-RYE-mah KAY-see"; read it off the table and you produce "tuh-ree-mah kah-seeh". The difference predicts whether a mamak counter understands you on the first try or the third.
